Monument-Valley-2.verdict: A short, beautiful puzzle game about impossible buildings, with no ads and no in-app purchases after the $3.99 price.
Monument-Valley-2.bestFor: Players who want a calm, polished puzzle game they can finish in a few evenings.
pros: One $3.99 payment, no ads and no in-app purchases
Clean, colorful art and soft music
Simple one-finger controls
Rated Everyone
cons: Fairly short, so it may be over quickly
Puzzles are gentle, so experienced puzzle fans may want more challenge
body: You guide a mother and her child through towers and temples built from impossible geometry. You tap to walk, drag handles and sliders, and rotate the structures until paths line up. There are no timers and no fail screens, so you can think at your own pace.

The story is small and told without much text. It follows the pair as the child grows more independent, and the levels reflect that. The look is bright and minimal, and nearly every screen would work as wallpaper.

If you like puzzles that are relaxing more than difficult, this is a good fit. It is also an easy pick for a first puzzle game or for sharing with family, since the price is clear and nothing interrupts you.
Monument-Valley-2.author: editors

Gardenscapes.verdict: A free match-3 game where each level you clear helps you restore a run-down garden.
Gardenscapes.bestFor: Casual players who like match-3 levels with a light story and decorating on top.
pros: Free to download and rated Everyone
Match-3 levels are easy to learn
Restoring the garden gives you a goal beyond the puzzles
Listed with no ads
cons: In-app purchases are available for boosters and extra lives
Progress is gated by stars and energy, so you may wait or pay
Later levels can become hard enough to push you toward spending
body: You swap tiles to match three or more, clearing the goals for each level. Winning gives you stars, and you spend those stars on garden tasks such as fixing fountains, planting flowers and choosing between a few design options. A butler named Austin guides you through the story.

The mix works well for short sessions. A level takes a few minutes, and a new garden task is often only a level or two away. The match-3 part stays familiar, with boosters and special tiles that you build as you play.
It suits people who enjoy slow, steady progress and don't mind the free-to-play pacing. If you dislike waiting for lives or being offered purchases, expect some of that here.
Gardenscapes.author: editors

Mini-Metro.verdict: A minimalist game where you draw subway lines for a growing city, for just $0.99.
Mini-Metro.bestFor: Players who like calm, thoughtful strategy and quick runs that you can replay.
pros: Only $0.99, with no ads and no in-app purchases
Easy to learn: you draw lines between stations
Each run plays out differently
Clean, simple look that is easy to read
cons: Runs always end when the network gets overloaded, which can feel harsh
Little story or long-term progress compared with bigger sim games
body: You start with a few stations shaped like circles, triangles and squares, and you connect them by dragging lines. Passengers appear wanting to travel to a station of a matching shape. As new stations pop up, you have to reroute lines and use the limited trains and tunnels you are given.
The challenge is in the planning. A layout that works early can jam later, so you keep redrawing as the city grows. Runs end when stations overcrowd, then you try again with a better idea.
It suits anyone who likes puzzle-like planning without a lot of menus. At $0.99 with no ads or purchases, it is a low-risk pick for short breaks.
Mini-Metro.author: editors

Toca-Life-World-Build-a-Story.verdict: A open-ended digital dollhouse where kids create their own characters, places and stories.
Toca-Life-World-Build-a-Story.bestFor: Younger children who enjoy pretend play and making up their own stories.
pros: Free to download and rated Everyone
No goals or scores, so kids set their own pace
Lots of characters and places to mix together
Listed with no ads
cons: Many extra locations and items are sold through in-app purchases
No set goals, so some kids may get bored
Parents may want to set limits on purchases
body: Toca Boca World is a sandbox. You move characters between homes, shops, schools and other places, and you can change how they look, what they hold and what they do. You make the story yourself by tapping and dragging.
There are no levels, timers or fail states. That makes it friendly for young kids, and the free version includes enough to start playing. More locations and extras can be bought in the app.
It works best for children who like pretend play, and it can be fun for older kids who like to build scenes. Parents should be aware of the store before handing over the device.
Toca-Life-World-Build-a-Story.author: editors

Homescapes.verdict: A free match-3 game where you renovate a family home room by room.
Homescapes.bestFor: Match-3 fans who enjoy decorating and a light family storyline.
pros: Free to download and rated Everyone
Renovating rooms gives your match-3 wins a clear purpose
Short levels fit quick breaks
Listed with no ads
cons: In-app purchases are available for boosters and lives
Lives and progress limits can slow you down
Gets harder over time, which may tempt you to spend
body: You play match-3 levels to earn stars, then use stars to renovate rooms in a big family house. The story follows butler Austin and his parents as the house is fixed up. You often choose between a couple of designs for each item.
The levels use boosters and obstacles that grow more complex as you advance. It is easy to pick up for a few minutes, and the renovation tasks give you a new goal after most levels.
It suits casual players who like an easy puzzle loop with decorating. If you do not like free-to-play limits, be ready for lives and the option to buy extras.
Homescapes.author: editors

Unblock-Me-Premium.verdict: A simple sliding-block puzzle for $0.99 where you clear a path for the red block.
Unblock-Me-Premium.bestFor: Anyone who wants easy-to-learn brain teasers for short breaks.
pros: Only $0.99 and listed with no ads
Rules take seconds to learn
Short puzzles suit quick play
Rated Everyone
cons: In-app purchases are listed, such as for hints
The idea stays the same, so it can feel repetitive
Harder puzzles may need patience or trial and error
body: Each puzzle is a grid of wooden blocks. You slide them up, down or sideways to make room, then guide the red block out through the exit. The controls are just dragging with your finger.
Early puzzles are quick, and they ramp up into ones that need several steps of planning. There is no story or art to speak of, so the appeal is the logic itself.
It fits people who like short puzzle sessions during a commute or waiting. You pay once up front, but check the store if you are thinking of buying hints.
Unblock-Me-Premium.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys.verdict: A tense horror game where you watch cameras and manage power while animatronics approach your office.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys.bestFor: Teens and adults who like jump-scare horror and can handle repeated tries.
pros: One-time $2.99 price and listed with no ads
Simple controls with tension that builds each night
Short sessions suit playing in the dark
Famous horror setup with a lot of lore to explore
cons: Rated Teen because of jump scares and horror
In-app purchases are listed
Repeating a night after a failure can be frustrating
body: You play a night security guard in a pizza restaurant. You sit in an office, check security cameras, close doors and use lights, all while your limited power drains. The animatronic characters move around between checks, and you have to guess when they are coming.

The game is about managing information and nerves. You have very few actions, so each decision matters, and the five nights get harder as they go. Failing usually means a sudden scare and starting the night again.
It suits players who like horror and learning patterns. If you scare easily or are buying for a younger child, note the Teen rating.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys-2.verdict: A sequel with more animatronics and no doors, so you rely on a mask and a wind-up music box.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-2.bestFor: Fans of the first game who want a harder, busier version of the same idea.
pros: One-time $2.99 price and listed with no ads
Adds new tools, including a Freddy mask and a music box
More characters to track keeps you alert
Fits short sessions
cons: Rated Teen because of horror and jump scares
In-app purchases are listed
More to juggle at once, so it can feel stressful or hard
body: Once again you are a night guard, but this time there are no doors to close. You wear a mask to fool some animatronics, use a flashlight on others, and keep winding a music box that must not stop. Several characters can threaten you at once, so you jump between tasks.

That makes it a busier game than the original. You need to remember who is coming from which direction and what each one responds to. The nights rise in difficulty and failing sends you back to the start of the night.
It is a good pick if you finished the first game and want something tougher. Newcomers can start here, but the Teen rating and the scares are worth thinking about.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-2.author: editors

Coloring-Book---Games-for-Kids.verdict: A free coloring app for kids with tap-to-fill pictures and simple drawing tools.
Coloring-Book---Games-for-Kids.bestFor: Young children who like to color and are playing with a parent nearby.
pros: Free to download and rated Everyone
Easy for small children to use
Listed with no ads
Relaxing activity with no pressure
cons: In-app purchases are available for extra content
Free content may feel limited after a while
Tapping to fill leaves less room for creativity than drawing by hand
body: Kids pick a picture and fill it with colors, using a palette and basic tools. It is quiet, simple and has no goals or timers. A child can spend a few minutes or much longer on one picture.
The controls are made for small hands, with big areas to tap. It is more about enjoying colors than learning to draw, which suits younger children best.
It makes a decent free option for car rides or quiet time. Parents should check what is locked behind purchases before handing the device to a child.
Coloring-Book---Games-for-Kids.author: editors

Monument-Valley.verdict: A short, artful puzzle game about Ida and impossible architecture, and a good place to start the series.
Monument-Valley.bestFor: Players who want a gentle puzzle game with striking visuals and a one-time price.
pros: Inventive puzzles built on optical illusions
Beautiful art and relaxing music
Easy touch controls
Listed with no ads and rated Everyone
cons: Short, so you can finish it in a couple of sittings
In-app purchases are listed, such as for extra chapters
Puzzles are mostly easy, so there is little challenge for experts
body: You guide a princess named Ida through buildings that bend the rules of space. By rotating towers, sliding platforms and changing your viewpoint, you can link paths that seem unconnected. Tapping is all you do to move her.

The puzzles teach you each new trick as it appears, so it rarely gets frustrating. The story is told lightly with minimal text, and the look is clean and colorful. It lasts only a short while, which is part of its charm.
It is a good fit if you like atmosphere and clever ideas more than tough challenges. At $3.99, it is a solid choice for a quiet evening.
Monument-Valley.author: editors

Bloons-TD-6.verdict: A deep tower defense game where you place monkeys and upgrades to pop waves of balloons.
Bloons-TD-6.bestFor: Strategy fans who want lots of content and are fine paying $6.99 up front.
pros: Many towers, upgrade paths and heroes to mix
Plenty of maps and modes for long-term play
Easy to start, but gets challenging
Listed with no ads and rated Everyone
cons: Costs $6.99, higher than most mobile games
In-app purchases are listed, such as for currency and extras
Hard modes can be demanding and need trial and error
body: You place monkey towers along a track to pop balloons before they reach the end. Each tower has upgrade paths that change how it works, and you can add heroes who level up during a match. Money earned by popping balloons pays for more towers and upgrades.

The early rounds are easy, then the balloons become tougher with new types and speeds. Finding combinations of towers that cope with them is the heart of the game. Different maps and difficulty settings give you reasons to come back and try new setups.
It suits both newcomers to tower defense and people who like to optimize. You pay up front, but there are no ads, and the amount to explore is large.
Bloons-TD-6.author: editors

Bloons-TD-5.verdict: An earlier Bloons tower defense game that is fun and straightforward, but it has ads as well as a price.
Bloons-TD-5.bestFor: Tower defense fans who want a simpler Bloons game and can put up with ads.
pros: Clear tower defense gameplay that is easy to learn
Plenty of towers and upgrades
Cheaper at $2.99
Rated Everyone
cons: Has ads even though it costs $2.99
In-app purchases are listed
Older design than Bloons TD 6 with less variety
body: As in other Bloons games, you place monkey towers and upgrade them to stop balloons from crossing the map. Earning money from popped balloons lets you build more defenses, and special towers and powers help in tough rounds.
The core idea is easy to pick up and fits both short and long sessions. The balloons get tougher as rounds go on, so you rethink your layout often.
It is a fair pick if you like the series and want a lower price. Because it has ads and purchases, many players will find Bloons TD 6 a smoother experience if they can afford the higher price.
Bloons-TD-5.author: editors

method: {site} recommends Android games from Google Play. Each game gets a score out of 5, shown next to its entry in our lists.
Editor's Choice is the label we give to a game we put at the top of a list as the best fit for that list's theme. A game can be an Editor's Choice in one list and not in another.

Ratings, install counts, prices, ads information and in-app purchase information come from Google Play. This data refreshes daily, so a game's details on {site} can change when its Google Play page changes.
The games are made by their developers, and you download them from Google Play. {site} is not affiliated with Google or with any game publisher.
Publishers do not pay for placement on {site}. A game appears in a list because we judged it a good fit for that list.
We revisit our lists regularly, adding or removing games when the details change or better fits appear.
